items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, three fence posts lean out of the moss at different heights. A groundskeeper strings one rope low for the toddlers, one higher for the parents, one higher still for the grandparents, refusing to leave until all three cross the same posts. The tangle reads as one family: three generations roped to the same ground.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, hand up before anyone asks, elbows in to fix the groundskeeper's ropes and gets both ankles lassoed for it. She yanks free, smooths her uniform, and announces the fix in one clipped syllable that sounds exactly like you'd <reading>say</reading> it: <reading>せい</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the improbable vending machine, the ground drops away and the valley opens below: field after field, boxed by its own low fence, patchworked to the horizon without a gap. It isn't one field anymore, it's every field at once, hemmed edge to edge, the boundaries adding up to the whole world.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker who dragged you up here, whom you've taken to calling <reading>Kai</reading> for the noise he makes at every switchback, doubles over at the summit and lets out one long <reading>かい</reading> of relief before he even looks at the view.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, the flagpole has bent sideways overnight. Sei drags it upright, braces it with her shoe, and raps it flat-handed with a pointer each time it slumps, until the whole field stands at attention around one stick beaten perfectly straight. That correcting by force is politics: government as the art of straightening what keeps slumping.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei doesn't stop at the flagpole. She marches the whole class into rows and claps them straight, and every clap lands on the same syllable, sharp as a ruler on a desk: <reading>せい</reading>, which you'd spell in English the way you'd <reading>say</reading> a drill sergeant's count.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the current thrashes every direction, slapping washing out of people's hands. Someone stacks flat stones into a low wall across the narrows, and the water that fought everyone all morning collects behind it into one flat, silent pool, obeying the wall completely. That taming of the flood is what this character means: to reign, to calm down.
items.reading_mnemonic: The stone-stacker, a quiet type the other kids call <reading>Ji</reading> because he never says more than one syllable, watches his pool go still and finally speaks: <reading>じ</reading>, and nothing else, satisfied.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In a hallway at Sei's school, picture the whole kanji as one image: a heavy iron lid clamped over a beating heart, muffling every thump. Pressure builds until the lid cracks a finger's width open, and a single bright spark hisses free through the gap — that spark, still hot, is the idea.
items.reading_mnemonic: That escaped spark turns out to be Eeko, a firefly who only ever says one sound. She loops once around the lockers and lets out a bright <reading>い</reading> — an <reading>eek</reading>-thin squeak of light — before ducking back through the crack in the lid to cool off.

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the fluorescent glare of Koichi's konbini, a customer catches his own reflection in the till's dark screen: upright on the left, but on the right the same body has folded double and sprouted a stubby tail. He watches, frozen, as one shape slides into the other, mid-blink — change.
items.reading_mnemonic: Outside the window, Kaa the fire-breathing crow has been watching the whole trick from the power line. He can't hold it in — he lets out a hoarse <reading>か</reading>, the same rasp as his name, <reading>Kaa</reading>, and a puff of flame scorches the wire above the sliding doors.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cat has fallen asleep spread-eagle across the mossy steps, arms flung wide and legs crossed at the ankle. Afternoon light slats through the eaves and lands across her fur in neat, deliberate lines, stroke after stroke, until her whole back reads as one finished sentence.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the rabbit twins, lean over the cat arguing about how it ends. One twin insists it needs a flourish on top, like a bread <reading>bun</reading>, and keeps hollering <reading>ぶん</reading> until the enormous bell rings and the cat twitches the whole sentence into a blur.

items.mnemonic_text: A nose pointing at oneself: 'me', self.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The staring <radical>eye</radical> that watches everything finally gets curious about itself. It swivels all the way around until it's pressed right up against a cracked mirror in Sei's school bathroom, pupil to pupil with its own reflection — recognizing, for the very first time, itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still at that mirror, a boy named <reading>Jeeves</reading> catches his own stare looking back and mutters <reading>じ</reading> — jeez — mortified that of everyone in the school, he's the one caught staring at himself.
items.description: 自 opens with a short diagonal tick above the top-left corner of the box — a stroke that 目 simply doesn't have; 目 is a plain, evenly-ruled rectangle with two level bars inside. 白 carries that same top tick, but its box is shorter and squarer with only a single centered bar, reading flatter and more compact than 自's taller, narrower frame.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末は自由です。
example_sentences.english: The weekend is free.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は自[じ]由[ゆう]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 自転車で公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the park by bicycle.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]で公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の自然はきれいです。
example_sentences.english: The mountain's nature is beautiful.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の自[し]然[ぜん]はきれいです。

items.mnemonic_text: An altar (示) marking earth (土): a shrine, and by extension a company.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On orientation day, the new hires drive the <radical>earth</radical> signpost into the ground behind Grandma Kane's shrine, right beside the stone <radical>altar</radical> where offerings sit out for everyone to see. Stake in the soil, altar in front of it — that's a company: a group planted on its own ground, showing itself off to the world.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still behind the shrine, a new hire named <reading>Shae</reading> trips over the freshly staked signpost and yelps <reading>しゃ</reading> as she stumbles face-first into the altar's offering tray — her first day at the company already the stuff of legend.
items.description: 社 originally named the local earth god's shrine — the altar raised on a patch of claimed ground for a village's protector spirit. The word later stretched to cover any group organized around a shared institution, which is why it equally means a shrine and a company: the modern sense kept the idea of a formal body bound to a place, not the religious content.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は会社で働いています。
example_sentences.english: My father works at a company.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は会[かい]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 姉は新聞社で働いています。
example_sentences.english: My older sister works at a newspaper company.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]は新[しん]聞[ぶん]社[しゃ]で働[はたら]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 社長はいつも忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: The company president is always busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 社[しゃ]長[ちょう]はいつも忙[いそが]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: An old man bent over a stick: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every day, the same stooped shuffle you know as <radical>old</radical> reappears at the crosswalk just as the sun climbs behind that little barred window marking a new <radical>day</radical>, and traffic idles while it crosses. Rain or shine, that shuffle is the one figure the neighborhood recognizes — not by name, just as a person who shows up every day.
items.reading_mnemonic: The driver stuck idling at that crosswalk, a man named <reading>Shuji</reading>, finally leans on his horn and shouts <reading>しゃ</reading> — shoo! — at the shuffling old figure, who doesn't even glance up before finishing the crossing at exactly the same pace.
items.description: 者 almost never stands alone as a word; it works as a suffix stitched onto a verb or field to name whoever does it, much the way English -er turns 'teach' into 'teacher'. Learning it as a floating idea of a person is the right starting point, but expect to meet it glued onto the end of something else far more often than by itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の母は医者です。
example_sentences.english: My mother is a doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の母[はは]は医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あの学者は有名です。
example_sentences.english: That scholar is famous.
example_sentences.furigana: あの学[がく]者[しゃ]は有[ゆう]名[めい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は科学者になりました。
example_sentences.english: He became a scientist.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は科[か]学[がく]者[しゃ]になりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the water doesn't get to wander. Picture the whole kanji as a stone flume bolted into the bank, forcing every drop of the river through one narrow channel, in the same order, with no shortcuts and no exceptions — that fixed channel, followed exactly, is the method.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hou, an owl who lives on the flume post, keeps watch for cheaters. Whenever a drop tries to leap the channel early, he swivels his head and hoots <reading>ほう</reading> — a low <reading>whoa</reading> that echoes off the water — until the drop falls back into line.

items.mnemonic_text: A workbench stacked with tools: one's trade, business.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> plants its four stiff legs on the level <radical>ground</radical> beneath a <radical>tree</radical>, hangs a little sign off a low branch, and spends the whole day there chewing calmly through paperwork, unbothered and punctual, running its own steady little trade. This is the sheep's business.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a regular customer named <reading>Geo</reading> strolls up to the sheep's stand under the tree, and the sheep bleats <reading>ぎょう</reading> back at him like a receipt stamping shut — same tree, same ground, same bleat, business as usual.

example_sentences.japanese: 授業の前に宿題をしました。
example_sentences.english: I did my homework before class.
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の前[まえ]に宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は来年大学を卒業します。
example_sentences.english: She's graduating from university next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は来[らい]年[ねん]大[だい]学[がく]を卒[そつ]業[ぎょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、残業があります。
example_sentences.english: I have overtime today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、残[ざん]業[ぎょう]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 利 as one tool: a thin blade lying flat beside a heavy stalk of grain, both leaning the same way, like a scale about to tip. At Koichi's konbini the clerk nicks a rice sack's string with that blade, and the sack weighs heavier after the cut than before. The register just prints profit.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the same konbini scale, the clerk keeps a dry <reading>reed</reading> tucked behind his ear for luck, and every time a sack outweighs itself he snaps the reed and grins, muttering a stretched <reading>り</reading> like he just got away with something.

items.meaning_mnemonic: See 務 as one overloaded figure: a spear on one shoulder, a stick raised in a striking hand, and one arm flexed hard under the weight — three demands crammed onto a single body, none optional. On the mountain trail the guide carries all three past every switchback, only dropping his shoulders at the vending machine on top. The task is done.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cow that wandered up years ago still blocks the trail near that vending machine until every task is read aloud to her. She answers each one with a flat <reading>moo</reading>, and that same flat sound is the reading <reading>む</reading> — one syllable, no complaints, task acknowledged.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 輸 as one vehicle: a wagon's two wheels bolted onto a hollowed dugout boat's hull, rolling the riverbank path and floating once the bank drops away. Crates get loaded on and it shoves off — wheels spinning uselessly underwater, hull scraping stone on land — yet the ugly thing drags everything across. That is transport.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman poling this contraption never learns anyone's name, so he calls every passenger the same drawn-out word as the wheels hit water: a long <reading>you</reading>. That same stretched syllable is the reading <reading>ゆ</reading>, hollered once as the crates lurch forward and the hull scrapes off from the bank.

items.meaning_mnemonic: See 格 as one gnarled tree at Grandma Kane's shrine, where each branch forks off at its own height and stops there, holding exactly one cat and no other — the top branch for the biggest cat, the lowest for the newest arrival. No cat may sit on a branch that isn't hers. That fixed, branch-by-branch order is status.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every visitor who climbs the shrine's mossy steps and sees the cats ranked branch by branch just stops and <reading>gawks</reading>, throat catching on the same flat sound as the reading <reading>かく</reading>. The shrine's one enormous bell seems to echo it back once for every branch in the tree.

items.mnemonic_text: A cloth over a stand where the city market gathers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You stroll into the town square and above every stall hangs a bright piece of <radical>cloth</radical> on a rod, snapping in the wind. On the biggest stall a pot steams away, and the vendor keeps slamming the flat disc of its <radical>lid</radical> back down over the rim so nobody smells the stew for free. Rows of cloth and clanging lids stretch as far as you can see. This is the heart of the city, its bustling market.
items.reading_mnemonic: The busiest stall belongs to Shi, a sharp-eyed vendor who greets every shopper crossing the market with a cheerful 「<reading>し</reading>!」. Follow her voice and you'll always find the center of the city.
items.description: Means city or market; shows up in words for towns and municipal places like 市 (city) and city names.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は去年からこの市に住んでいます。
example_sentences.english: I've been living in this city since last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は去[きょ]年[ねん]からこの市[し]に住[す]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 市の図書館は駅の隣にあります。
example_sentences.english: The city library is right next to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 市[し]の図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]は駅[えき]の隣[となり]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に市の公園を散歩しました。
example_sentences.english: I took a walk through the city park over the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に市[し]の公[こう]園[えん]を散[さん]歩[ぽ]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) inspected all over (侴): to test, examine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>horse</radical> gallops in, all boxy body and dust-kicking hooves, expecting a race. Instead a vet in a lab coat pins it to a scale, shines a light in its eyes, and checks its teeth one by one. The horse stamps and snorts, furious, but every inch of it gets examined before it's ever let out to run.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, guards the clinic door with a wall of antique blades gleaming behind him. Every time the horse tries to bolt past without finishing its checkup, Ken barks one sharp <reading>けん</reading> — <reading>Ken</reading> means nobody skips the exam.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日試験があります。
example_sentences.english: There's an exam tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]試[し]験[けん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は毎週実験をします。
example_sentences.english: She does an experiment every week.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は毎[まい]週[しゅう]実[じっ]験[けん]をします。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生は図書館で試験を受けます。
example_sentences.english: The student takes the exam at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]は図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で試[し]験[けん]を受[う]けます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 工 as a squat steel I-beam — flat cap on top, flat foot on the bottom, one spine welded straight down the middle. A crew winches it upright on a bare lot and bolts it in before a single wall exists. That lone beam is the first thing raised on any job site: the shape of craft itself, construction standing on end.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi wheels his restocking cart past the freshly bolted beam and clips his elbow on the corner. He lets out a flat <reading>coo</reading>, dragging the vowel out long like his till's slow beep: <reading>こう</reading>. Then he reroutes the onigiri delivery around it.

items.mnemonic_text: A field (田) sitting over the heart (心): thoughts forming.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You stand at the edge of your flooded <radical>rice field</radical>, its paths crossing the plots into a grid below you. Above it your wounded <radical>heart</radical> drags itself up and hovers there, thumping, while you stare at the grid, turning the harvest over one square at a time. That thumping stillness is what it looks like to think.
items.reading_mnemonic: A heron named Shi stands dead still over the rice field, chewing over something enormous. Every few minutes it snaps its beak and lets out one flat <reading>し</reading> — proof that all that stillness is <reading>Shi</reading>'s thought, not sleep.

example_sentences.japanese: この本はどう思いますか。
example_sentences.english: What do you think of this book?
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]はどう思[おも]いますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はそう思います。
example_sentences.english: I think so.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はそう思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は忙しいと思います。
example_sentences.english: I think she's busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は忙[いそが]しいと思[おも]います。

items.mnemonic_text: A bow (弓) with its string pulled taut: to pull.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the improbable vending machine, an archer plants their feet and hauls back on a springy <radical>bow</radical>, bending its stacked-curve wood taut until the string bites into their fingers. That single act of hauling back is the whole meaning: to pull.
items.reading_mnemonic: A parrot named Inko perches on the vending machine and screeches <reading>いん</reading> the instant the string snaps taut, like an <reading>inn</reading> bell ringing for a guest who arrived too fast. Every hiker on the trail flinches at the sound before they even see the arrow.

example_sentences.japanese: 引き出しの中に鍵があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a key inside the drawer.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]き出[だ]しの中[なか]に鍵[かぎ]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、家族で引っ越します。
example_sentences.english: Next month, my family and I are moving.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、家[か]族[ぞく]で引[ひ]っ越[こ]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 割引で靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought the shoes at a discount.
example_sentences.furigana: 割[わり]引[びき]で靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 点 as a hanko stamped too hard onto a test paper in the school's front hall. The seal bursts and four fat ink droplets spatter sideways across the score box. Each droplet dries into its own dark, unmistakable dot — a spot pressed into the page, a mark nobody can argue with.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hall monitor everyone just calls <reading>Ten</reading> finds the spattered test on the floor and holds up all ten fingers, hissing <reading>てん</reading> like he's counting the ink spots one by one before confiscating the paper.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 原 as a slab of white rock jutting low over the mountain trail, a thin spring bleeding out from underneath it, unstoppable, spreading downhill until the ground finally opens into a flat meadow of undisturbed grass. This is where the trail's only water starts — the meadow, the original spot everything downstream traces back to.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker named <reading>Gen</reading> kneels at the spring to refill her bottle, and the cold hits her wrist so hard she yelps <reading>げん</reading>, sharp enough that the grasshoppers in the meadow scatter for cover.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 婦 as a woman named Fumi sweeping Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps at dawn in a long apron, her broom scraping stone in the same rhythm every morning while the shrine cats scatter out of her path. She works the steps top to bottom without once looking up — the picture of a lady running her own household, corner by corner.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine gate, Fumi leans her broom against the rail and blows out a long <reading>phew</reading>, a breathy <reading>ふ</reading> that scatters the incense smoke, before picking the broom back up to finish the steps.

items.meaning_mnemonic: 性 shows up as one stamped box on a school health form: the box for your inborn nature, whatever you were born as. Sei, always first to raise his hand, isn't satisfied checking it once — he stamps it three times and asks the nurse to grade his nature like an exam. Stamped and graded: that is your sex, your gender, your nature.
items.reading_mnemonic: The nurse, exhausted, waves the form away and tells him to just <reading>say</reading> his name and leave — Sei straightens up and corrects her anyway: it's <reading>せい</reading>, properly stamped, thank you.

items.mnemonic_text: An arrow (矢) hitting the mouth's (口) point: to know for certain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, an <radical>arrow</radical> streaks straight across the grass and thunks dead center into the target, and in that same instant your <radical>mouth</radical> snaps open with the answer — no hesitation, just the fact flying out as fast and true as the shot. That instant, certain hit is knowing something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chibi the parrot roosts on that same target and shrieks <reading>ち</reading> the second the arrow lands, confirming the answer before you can even say it out loud — a sharp <reading>chee</reading> of certainty every time.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はその人を知りません。
example_sentences.english: I don't know that person.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はその人[ひと]を知[し]りません。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生が私たちに知らせました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher let us know.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]が私[わたし]たちに知[し]らせました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はすぐに承知しました。
example_sentences.english: He agreed right away.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はすぐに承[しょう]知[ち]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: Small (小) with a slash taken off: even fewer.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take something <radical>small</radical> — that hook with two flanking dots — and slice one more dot away with a downward stroke. Now there's even less than small: barely anything left. When you take a bite out of small, what remains is few.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, opens his white-gloved hand to reveal only a few crumbs of confetti — "<reading>しょう</reading> time!" he squeaks, and even the doves look unimpressed by how little there is. His whole act, like everything about him, is small and few.
items.description: 少 is 小 with one extra stroke: a slash sweeping down and to the left below the base. Take that tail away and you are back to 小.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は少し寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It's a little cold today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は少[すこ]し寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この本は少し高いです。
example_sentences.english: This book is a little expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は少[すこ]し高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本語を少し話します。
example_sentences.english: I speak a little Japanese.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]語[ご]を少[すこ]し話[はな]します。

items.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, and underneath it a <radical>right hand</radical> comes up to meet it. Two hands reaching in from opposite directions and closing on each other. Nobody is being paid for this and nobody is in charge of anybody. That is a <radical>friend</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is the one who is always there before you, hand already out, drawing the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have even shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank the water sits mirror-still: a hiker leans over and his reflection leans back at the same angle, matching every twitch. He waves, the water waves back; he frowns, it frowns back — two sides doing the same thing to each other, neither one first. That two-way mirroring is 相: inter-, mutual, together.
items.reading_mnemonic: The hiker, Sou, leans in close and mutters <reading>そう</reading> to his own reflection, daring it to answer — and right on cue, impossibly, the water mutters <reading>so</reading> straight back at him, word for word, syllable for syllable.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine atop the mountain trail is the only comfort after that whole steep climb, and a hiker treats it like a hotel lobby: he drops his pack, kicks off his boots, and waits for someone to bring him tea. Mountain or not, he has appointed himself the honored guest, expecting service and a seat — 客: guest, visitor, customer.
items.reading_mnemonic: His ride up was a foul-tempered <reading>yak</reading> that refuses to leave the summit now, planting itself by the machine like it's checked into a hotel — a guide radios down that a <reading>きゃく</reading> has arrived and shows no sign of ever checking out.

items.mnemonic_text: A road (辶) that splits away (韋): to differ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A disembodied <radical>mouth</radical> plants itself at a fork in the road and bellows directions with total confidence, left, while your own footsteps quietly <radical>advance</radical> right instead, because the mouth's directions never match where the road goes. Two opinions, two paths: that is what it means to differ.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named <reading>E</reading> takes the mouth's directions and immediately regrets it, stubbing her toe on a root and yelping <reading>い</reading>, which is exactly the sound of finding out, one more time, that the two of you always end up disagreeing.

items.mnemonic_text: A knife (刂) cutting a shape (另) apart: to separate.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi never locks the konbini doors — day, night, holiday, no difference — because in his head the shop stopped being his years ago and became everyone's. He restocks the onigiri shelf for total strangers like a prince tending his domain, open to anyone who walks in. That is 公: public, official, everyone's business.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regulars don't bother with his whole name anymore — they just call out the long stretched <reading>Ko</reading> of 'Koichi' as he blurs past restocking, and it comes out as one clipped <reading>こう</reading>, because efficiency belongs to the public queue, not to small talk.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two matching wooden panels, hinged and identical, standing across from each other at Grandma Kane's shrine, flanking the mossy steps. A cat darts between them and both panels swing shut at once, clapping together with a boom that sets the enormous bell ringing. Twin doors that only work as a pair — that's a gate.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, argue at Grandma Kane's shrine, each ending every sentence with a flat <reading>もん</reading> — book-nerd slang for obviously. They stand together like the gate's own twin panels, and every <reading>Mon</reading> makes the enormous bell shiver on its hook.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one battered vending machine waits by the summit sign. A hiker feeds it a coin, and instead of a drink, the whole machine shudders, its panels folding and reforming until it isn't a vending machine anymore — it's a wooden bench, still warm. That's turn into: one thing reshaping into another.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei reaches the summit first, hand up before anyone can ask, and plants herself by the vending machine that just turned into a bench. She declares it like a quiz answer: a crisp, smug <reading>せい</reading>, and hikers who arrive late swear they can still hear that <reading>say</reading> echo off the rocks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer holds up an onigiri with the label torn clean off and asks what's inside. The clerk squints at it, sniffs it once, then waves a hand vaguely at the whole shelf — sort of like those, probably that kind of thing. Nobody presses further; sort of thing turns out to be a real answer here.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk, whom regulars just call <reading>Zen</reading> for his permanent shrug, mutters a flat <reading>ぜん</reading> every time someone asks for specifics, sliding the mystery onigiri back onto the shelf without another word. Say his name fast enough and it collapses into the same flat <reading>ぜん</reading> — shrug included.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, something pale and square drifts down with the current — a blank wooden mask, one oval outline, two carved eye-holes. Someone wades in, fishes it out, and holds it right over their own face. Their expression vanishes, replaced by the mask's flat stare. That's a mask — a face swapped for a face.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman who drags it from the water, everyone calls him <reading>Men</reading> for the grunt he gives instead of talking, holds the mask to the sky and lets out a low <reading>めん</reading> like a verdict. From then on, every mask pulled from that river gets the same flat <reading>めん</reading> before anyone's allowed to touch it.

items.mnemonic_text: Big (大) with an extra drop of size: thick, fat.

A single <radical>drop</radical> - a ladle of stew, not water - plops right onto his belly and soaks straight in. His stomach swells outward on the spot, arms pushed even wider by his own gut. That one dropped ladle is the difference between big and thick, fat.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cook who ladled that stew is a heavyset chef named <reading>Tai</reading>. He pats his own swollen belly, proud of the extra drop he added, and sighs <reading>たい</reading>, satisfied at how thick he's made himself.
items.description: 太 is 大 (big) with one extra dot. On 太 that dot sits low, tucked between the legs where the stew dripped in - the mark of something thickened. On 犬 (dog) the dot instead sits high, off the right arm, like a tail flicked up and out. Same big-person shape, different spot for the single drop.

items.reading_mnemonic: The ox pulling the scale, a stubborn animal named <reading>Joo</reading>, plants its hooves and refuses to shift. Villagers push and it just groans <reading>じゅう</reading>, sinking deeper into the ground instead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Rain floods the school's sports field mid-relay, runners skidding through mud while the crowd groans under dripping umbrellas. items.reading_mnemonic: As the sky clears, Sei's hand shoots up first as always, uniform spotless despite the mud, and she announces it to the whole field, loud and smug: <reading>せい</reading> — like she's the one who <reading>said</reading> the sky would clear.

items.mnemonic_text: An upright frame with pupils inside: an eye.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's an upright frame with two pupils sitting inside it. Tip it on its side and it even looks like it's staring right back at you. That frame with pupils is exactly what it is — an <radical>eye</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woodcarver named <reading>もく</reading> is whittling a tiny wooden eye at Koichi's konbini counter, holding it up to inspect the grain. Every time he blinks, he mutters "もく, もく" as he lines the carving up with his own eye.
items.description: Count the bars inside the box. 目 is tall with two horizontals. 日 has one. 自 is 目 with a small slash added on top of the box.

items.reading_mnemonic: The boy's only witness is Sow, a pig who lives by the crossing, and every time he lobs a parcel over the water she gives the same unimpressed grunt, <reading>そう</reading> — which sounds exactly like someone muttering <reading>so</reading> to themselves right before they let something go.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the microwave runs three full cycles on one forgotten onigiri, the wrapper bubbling and warping, the till beeping in panic behind the counter. items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk mopping her forehead at the register is nicknamed <reading>Netsu</reading> for it, and every time that wall of heat rolls out she groans the sound of her own name, <reading>ねつ</reading>, dragging it out like she's wading through hot fishing nets.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A stiff figure plants itself at the top of Grandma Kane's mossy steps, arms flung straight out, ankles crossed tight, blocking the path to the enormous bell. Cats stream around its legs but it will not move, will not ring, will not budge — every request meets the same flat refusal. Negative.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat everyone calls <reading>Fu</reading>, curled against the stubborn figure's crossed feet, doesn't hiss so much as sigh through her nose — a flat little <reading>ふ</reading> of a breath, unimpressed by every visitor who tries to squeeze past.
items.description: This kanji almost never stands alone in real sentences; you meet it glued to the front of other words as a flat negation prefix, closer to un- or non- in English than a standalone word for bad.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) safe under a roof: peaceful and cheap.

items.reading_mnemonic: She's spreading sweet red <reading>あん</reading> (bean paste) on a bun, humming, utterly at peace. Every bite is cheap comfort — say あん and taste that calm.
items.description: 安 means cheap or peaceful, and shows up in words for low prices, safety, and being at ease.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail narrows to a knife-edge ridge, the path pinching to nothing between two sheer drops, one wrong step from the vending machine improbably waiting at the top. items.reading_mnemonic: Guarding that narrow ledge is <reading>Ken</reading>, the shiba who never leaves his wall of antique swords, and every hiker who eyes the vending machine past him gets one warning bark of <reading>けん</reading> before he bares a blade in his teeth.
items.description: Beyond the literal steep-cliff picture, this kanji usually carries a broader sense of danger or risk in real vocabulary — insurance, adventure, hazard — rather than physical steepness itself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the school sports field, the coach chalks one line across the track and rules that only a toe planted exactly on it counts. Every runner skids past it or stops short — except Sei, uniform still spotless, who lands a toe dead on the line without even trying, smug before the whistle even blows: correct.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back in the classroom, the teacher asks who stopped exactly on the line. Sei's hand shoots up before she finishes asking, and he answers with his own name like it settles it: <reading>Sei</reading>, <reading>せい</reading> — crisp, correct, a little too pleased with himself.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, everything bends — the reeds, the ripples, the rope holding the ferry to its post. Only the ferryman's eye stays fixed dead ahead on the far bank. items.reading_mnemonic: On the far bank, kids call the ferryman Chalky, because his pole is an actual stick of chalk that drags one straight white line across the water on every crossing. Ask him why and he barks the same flat answer every time: <reading>ちょく</reading>, <reading>chalk</reading> — straight, immediate, no explanation given.

items.reading_mnemonic: The apprentice threading the loom is named <reading>Kay</reading>, and every time the shuttle passes through she exhales a low <reading>けい</reading>, matching the monk's chant beat for beat until the thread and the sutra finish the row together.

items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that same signpost, a farmer named Zo watches the water creep higher up the wood and grunts <reading>ぞう</reading> each time — flat and low, like saying '<reading>zo</reading>' with a shrug. items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs the last onigiri off the shelf by the door and bites in before checking the date.
